title: Living ashtpadi 19

segments.voice: Yesterday, what does go, and your line: kindness travels. Did you take the first step of a lasting kindness? Today we take the whole nineteenth ashtpadi off the page and into the house. Day five hundred thirteen.

Every home has one. The drawer. Dead batteries, a takeout menu from a restaurant that closed, three keys to locks nobody remembers, a charger for a phone long gone. Nobody decided to keep any of it. It just collected, the way things do when nobody's looking. And every time you open that drawer looking for scissors, you have to dig. The nineteenth ashtpadi has spent three days on what stays behind and what goes along. Living it starts somewhere very small. Maybe with that drawer.
screen: `THE DRAWER EVERY HOME HAS.` → `IT JUST COLLECTED.` → `LIVING IT STARTS SMALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the nineteenth ashtpadi in one breath: the riches, youth and power we pile up stay behind; the Name we earn and the good we do go along. So how do people actually live that? Not, in Sikh teaching, by leaving home. Guru Nanak spent his last years farming at Kartarpur, raising a family, running a community kitchen. Sikhs call that life grihasti, the householder's path, and they hold it up as a full spiritual life. So living light doesn't mean owning nothing. It means owning lightly: holding things with an open hand. Guru Nanak gave a picture for it in the Sidh Gosht, his conversation with the Siddhas, the yogi masters. In paraphrase: as the lotus floats on the water and stays untouched by it, as the duck swims the stream and stays dry. Kamal, the lotus: it lives in the pond and isn't soaked by it. In the world, not drowned in it. And then there's the drawer. It may seem silly to link a junk drawer to a hymn, but Sukhmani works on the mind, and the mind is often cluttered in exactly that way: old grudges, worries about things that never happened, plans for a version of life you outgrew. Clearing a drawer won't clear all that. But it's practice. You learn to look at something, admit you're not using it, and let it go to someone who will. That's living light: not empty hands, open ones.
screen: `STAYS BEHIND, GOES ALONG.` · `NOT RUNNING AWAY: THE HOUSEHOLDER.` · `THE LOTUS: IN THE WATER, NOT SOAKED.` · `THE DRAWER: PRACTICE LETTING GO.` · then, large: `OPEN HANDS, NOT EMPTY ONES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clear out one drawer. If you can, go to it now. If you can't, picture it clearly. Take out one thing at a time and hold it for a breath. Ask: do I use this? Could someone else? Make three small piles: keep, give, throw away. Don't hurry, and don't judge yourself for what's in there. Just notice how the hand opens a little more each time. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as each thing goes. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi 19. The householder's way: owning lightly, like the lotus on the water, and letting go of what you don't use so it can move on.
Your line: live light. Today, take the give pile somewhere it will be used: a donation box, a neighbor, a friend who needs a charger. Day five hundred thirteen.
